name: Oxymetazoline eye drops (Upneeq)

card.summary: A prescription 0.1% oxymetazoline eye drop approved for acquired ptosis that lifts the lid slightly; forum users discuss cheaper nasal-spray substitutes, which are not the approved product.
card.note: Nasal-spray substitutes are not the approved eye formulation; ask a clinician.

quick.overview:
Upneeq is oxymetazoline hydrochloride 0.1% ophthalmic solution, approved by the FDA in July 2020 for acquired blepharoptosis in adults. Oxymetazoline is also long used in nasal decongestant sprays and redness eye drops.
Its appearance use is a brief lift of a mildly drooping upper lid for a more open look. On looksmax.org, users have asked whether nasal spray can substitute because Upneeq is costly and hard to obtain in Europe.
quick.mechanism: Oxymetazoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist; for ptosis it is thought to stimulate receptors in Muller's muscle, which raises the lid.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes rebound congestion and dependence with nasal oxymetazoline. Nasal spray is formulated for the nose; clinicians' views on its use in the eye are not documented.

lead: Upneeq is a brand of 0.1% oxymetazoline hydrochloride ophthalmic solution, approved by the US FDA in July 2020 to treat acquired blepharoptosis, a droop of the upper eyelid. Used as a once-daily drop, it raises the lid slightly, which opens the eye and can make the eyes look more awake and symmetrical without surgery.[5][8] Oxymetazoline is an imidazoline-derivative alpha-adrenergic agonist developed from xylometazoline at Merck in 1961 and is also used in nasal sprays, redness drops and a rosacea cream.[5]

For ptosis the drug is thought to act on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors in Muller's muscle, the sympathetically controlled superior tarsal muscle that helps elevate the upper lid. The label describes the lid-margin lift as peaking about two hours after the drop and remaining raised through eight hours.[5][7][8] It has also been described in published case reports for lid droop after botulinum toxin treatment, and a 2025 case series proposed using it as a trial before deciding on surgery.[1][11]

The approval rested on two randomized, double-masked, vehicle-controlled trials of about six weeks that enrolled 304 adults and measured the upper visual field and lid position, and a 2025 meta-analysis of four randomized trials with 448 participants reported a greater lid-margin lift than placebo.[8][9]

In looksmaxxing forums Upneeq is discussed as a way to get a more open eye, with threads centred on its cost and availability outside the US and on whether cheaper oxymetazoline products can substitute.[6] The approved product is a dedicated ophthalmic solution; no published study has tested nasal sprays in the eye.
infobox: Lid lift peaks about 2 hours after the drop and persists through 8 hours[8]
Prescription in the US for ophthalmic ptosis; nasal oxymetazoline is OTC[5]

paras: Approved use is acquired blepharoptosis in adults.[5] Published reports describe oxymetazoline 0.1% together with pretarsal botulinum toxin for severe botulinum-induced ptosis.[1] Wikipedia lists other oxymetazoline uses as nasal decongestion, eye redness and facial redness in rosacea.[5]
Other approved oxymetazoline products include nasal decongestant sprays, Visine L.R. redness drops, and Rhofade 1% cream for persistent facial redness in rosacea, approved by FDA in January 2017.[5]

In practice Upneeq is a diagnostic and bridging option as well as a cosmetic one. A 2025 Cureus case series of five patients proposed an algorithm in which a good lid response to oxymetazoline points toward internal ptosis repair and a weak response toward external repair, and the authors describe the drop as both a diagnostic tool and a bridge before surgery.[11] They contrast it with older eye drops such as apraclonidine and phenylephrine, which they describe as having more notable side effects.[11]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: The effect people want is a modest lift of the upper lid margin, which exposes more of the iris and can reduce the heavy-lidded or tired look and some asymmetry between the eyes. The label describes use as a once-daily drop in each affected eye, and its pharmacology section says the lift is measured by marginal reflex distance (MRD1), the distance from the pupil's light reflex to the upper lid edge.[8] The label reports the lift as measurable through eight hours after a dose.[8]

Dermatology and aesthetic-medicine authors discuss the drop in the context of botulinum toxin treatments, where spread of the toxin to the lid-raising muscle can cause a temporary droop. A 2023 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper describes combining oxymetazoline 0.1% with pretarsal botulinum toxin for severe cases.[1]

sections.h: Ptosis and why the lid matters for appearance
paras: Acquired ptosis most commonly results from aponeurotic changes, in which the levator aponeurosis weakens or detaches with age; other causes include chronic inflammation, intraocular surgery, trauma, tumours and Horner syndrome, which damages the sympathetic supply to Muller's muscle and typically produces mild ptosis of no more than 2 mm.[7] Clinicians quantify droop by the marginal reflex distance, the distance from the pupil centre to the upper lid edge.[7]

Wikipedia notes that surgery, including levator resection, Muller's muscle resection and sling procedures, may be recommended when appearance is a concern even if vision is not significantly affected; risks include asymmetry, dry eye, bleeding, infection and, rarely, loss of lid movement.[7] Non-surgical supports include ptosis crutches and scleral lenses.[7] A drop that lifts the lid slightly is therefore positioned between doing nothing and a surgical procedure.
Oxymetazoline mainly activates alpha-1 and partly alpha-2 adrenergic receptors; in ptosis these actions in Muller's muscle are thought to elevate the lid.[5]

Oxymetazoline selectively activates alpha-1 and partially activates alpha-2 receptors; in nasal use effects begin within minutes and last up to six hours, with an elimination half-life of about 5 to 8 hours and about 30 percent excreted unchanged in urine.[5]

The compound was developed from xylometazoline at Merck by Wolfgang Fruhstorfer and Helmut Muller-Calgan in 1961; Afrin was first sold as a prescription nasal product in 1966 and became over the counter in 1975.[5]

Oxymetazoline itself dates to 1961, when Wolfgang Fruhstorfer and Helmut Muller-Calgan developed it from xylometazoline at Merck; Afrin was first sold as a prescription nasal product in 1966 and became over the counter in 1975.[5] The FDA approved a 1% oxymetazoline cream for persistent facial redness in rosacea in January 2017.[5]

In July 2020 the FDA approved oxymetazoline 0.1% ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis in adults, and the label lists an August 21, 2020 marketing start.[5][8] Reviews and registered trials since then have looked at its effect on lid position, eye appearance and ptosis from facial nerve conditions, with a head-to-head Upneeq versus Lumify ptosis trial registered for a 2026 start.[2][3][4][9]

The prescribing information describes two randomized, double-masked, vehicle-controlled, parallel-group trials, each lasting 42 days with about 2:1 randomization to Upneeq or vehicle. Trial 1 randomized 140 adults (mean age 64) and trial 2 randomized 164 (mean age 63). The primary endpoint was the change in points seen on the upper four rows of the Leicester Peripheral Field Test; the increase was statistically significant versus vehicle at day 1 (6 hours after the dose) and day 14 (2 hours after the dose), and MRD1 rose more with Upneeq than vehicle at the same time points.[8]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Clinical Ophthalmology pooled four randomized placebo-controlled trials with 448 participants, finding a greater MRD1 increase than placebo and no significant difference in serious adverse events (1.2 percent versus 1.6 percent).[9] A completed Phase 4 study of Upneeq on eyelid position, eye redness and eye appearance enrolled 114 participants.[2]

The Upneeq label lists reactions in 1 to 5 percent of 360 treated subjects, namely punctate keratitis, conjunctival redness, dry eye, blurred vision, pain on instillation, eye irritation and headache.[8] Its warnings note that ptosis can be a sign of neurologic or orbital disease (stroke, aneurysm, Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis or an orbital mass), that as an alpha-adrenergic agonist the drug may affect blood pressure, that caution applies in cerebral or coronary insufficiency and Sjogren syndrome, and that it may raise the risk of angle-closure glaucoma in people with untreated narrow angles. The label also advises that the container tip should not touch the eye or any surface.[8]

A 2026 analysis of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System in Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery examined 306 patients with 658 reported events from 2020 to April 2025. It confirmed labeled events, with ocular surface disease the most common, and flagged signals not on the label, including retinal and vitreous complications, dilated pupil, hypertension and loss of effect over time; the authors state that further studies are needed to confirm these associations.[10]

For nasal oxymetazoline, Wikipedia reports rebound congestion and describes a moderate dependence liability, with a 2006 review recommending limiting nasal use to three days; repeated intranasal use beyond three to five days can lead to recurrent congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa), and intranasal glucocorticoids are known to help treat it.[5]

For specific groups, the label reports no human pregnancy data, no clinical lactation data, and no established safety or effectiveness in patients under 13; 315 subjects aged 65 and older were studied, with no overall differences from younger subjects.[8]

Wikipedia lists oxymetazoline brands including Afrin, Otrivin, Dristan, Vicks Sinex, Visine L.R., Rhofade for the cream and Upneeq for the ophthalmic solution, and states that in the United Kingdom nasal oxymetazoline is on the General Sales List while in the United States nasal products are over the counter and the eye solution and cream are prescription-only.[5]

Ophthalmic Upneeq is a US-marketed brand, which accounts for the forum discussion about access in Europe.[6] Wikipedia also records that oxymetazoline was the 305th most commonly prescribed US medication in 2022 with more than 300,000 prescriptions, and that a topical formulation for hair loss (DA-020) was in preclinical development as of March 2026.[5]

Wikipedia's ptosis article describes the surgical alternatives as levator resection, Muller muscle resection and sling procedures, with non-surgical options including ptosis crutches and scleral contact lenses, and reports that the 2020 drop approval added a pharmacologic option.[7]

A looksmax.org poster said that Upneeq is very expensive and nearly impossible to obtain in Europe, and asked whether a nasal spray seen used as eye drops on Reddit could serve as an alternative and whether this would be safe.[6]

Registered trials include a completed Phase 4 study of Upneeq on eyelid position, eye redness and appearance (NCT04831047, 114 participants),[2] a completed Phase 3 trial of oxymetazoline for ptosis from synkinesis (NCT05945615, 36 participants),[3] and a planned Phase 4 comparison of Upneeq and Lumify for ptosis (NCT07390578).[4] A published report describes oxymetazoline for botulinum-induced ptosis.[1]

The Phase 4 Upneeq trial (NCT04831047) lists conditions of ptosis, conjunctival inflammation and eye appearance, and the synkinesis trial (NCT05945615) enrols people with facial paralysis and hyperkinesis.[2][3] The planned Upneeq versus Lumify comparison (NCT07390578) is designed for 50 participants with acquired ptosis and is not yet recruiting.[4]

A 2025 meta-analysis of randomized trials and the two pivotal vehicle-controlled trials summarized in the label are described in the Effectiveness section.[8][9] Case series, such as five patients treated with oxymetazoline and followed to build a treatment algorithm, add real-world detail.[11]

timeline.event: Oxymetazoline is developed at Merck by Fruhstorfer and Muller-Calgan.[5]
Afrin first sold as a prescription nasal product (OTC from 1975).[5]
FDA approves 1% oxymetazoline cream for rosacea redness.[5]
FDA approves oxymetazoline 0.1% ophthalmic solution (Upneeq) for acquired blepharoptosis in July; marketing starts in August.[5][8]
Phase 4 trial of Upneeq on eyelid position, eye redness and appearance begins (NCT04831047).[2]
Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper on oxymetazoline with pretarsal botulinum toxin for severe botulinum-induced ptosis.[1]
Phase 3 trial of oxymetazoline for ptosis from synkinesis begins (NCT05945615).[3]
Clinical Ophthalmology meta-analysis of four randomized trials (448 participants); Cureus case series proposes a treatment algorithm.[9][11]
FAERS pharmacovigilance analysis published; Upneeq versus Lumify ptosis trial registered.[4][10]

lore.intro: Discussion centres on cost, availability and whether nasal sprays can be substituted for the dedicated eye drop.[6]

claims.claim: A nasal spray can be used as an alternative to Upneeq eye drops.
claims.believers: A poster says Upneeq is expensive and hard to get in Europe and cites a Reddit user using nasal spray as drops.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested nasal spray in the eye; the approved product is a dedicated ophthalmic solution.[5][8]

claims.claim: Oxymetazoline drops give a lifted, more open eye without surgery.
claims.believers: Users discuss the drop as a surgery-free route to a more open eye and weigh its high price and limited availability in Europe.[6]
claims.experts: The FDA approved 0.1% oxymetazoline ophthalmic solution in 2020; the label's trials and a 2025 meta-analysis report greater lid lift than placebo.[5][8][9]

claims.claim: The lift is temporary and fades as the drop wears off.
claims.believers: Users compare it with surgery as a non-permanent, lower-commitment way to open the eye.[6]
claims.experts: The label reports lid-margin height peaking at about two hours and staying raised through eight hours.[8]

claims.claim: Oxymetazoline is a familiar drug, so eye use should be safe.
claims.believers: The poster asks whether a nasal-spray oxymetazoline product would be safe as eye drops.[6]
claims.experts: The label lists ocular and blood-pressure warnings, and a 2026 FAERS analysis flagged additional signals needing confirmation.[8][10]

chain: Oxymetazoline stimulates alpha receptors in Muller's muscle
Upper eyelid lifts a millimetre or so
Wider-looking, more open eye and less hooded appearance
angle.text: Users apply the drop to lift a drooping or hooded upper lid so the eye looks more open and awake. The effect is temporary and tied to continued use, in contrast to surgery.
